items.title: Four views on local travel
items.prompt: Read the four opinions. Match each statement to one person. You may choose a person more than once.

passages.heading: Amira
passages.text: I have started cycling to work, but I do not think everyone can do the same. My colleague has to take her children to two different places before her shift, so a bicycle would not solve her problem. For me, the main attraction is knowing how long my journey will take. Cars often sit in queues while I can keep moving. I would welcome safer junctions, although I would rather see the council improve existing routes than spend money on a large publicity campaign.

passages.heading: Ben
passages.text: I used to drive every day, but the new bus timetable changed my mind. There is now a service just after my evening shift ends. I still take the car when I visit my parents outside town because the bus journey there takes too long. I do not mind paying slightly more for a reliable service. What bothers me is not knowing whether the next bus will actually arrive. Accurate live information would make a bigger difference to me than colourful new vehicles.

passages.heading: Chloe
passages.text: My shop depends on customers who carry heavy bags, so I was worried when the council proposed closing our street to cars. After a trial weekend, however, sales increased because people stayed longer and explored the smaller shops. I now support the closure during busy shopping hours, provided deliveries are allowed early in the morning. A permanent ban on every vehicle at every hour would create problems. The council should speak to businesses about practical details before extending the scheme.

passages.heading: Daniel
passages.text: I enjoy walking and normally walk to the station. However, the cheapest bus ticket is a weekly one, which is poor value for someone like me who only needs a bus occasionally. A ticket that could be used on several separate days would be more useful. I would also like more benches along the walking route. These would help older neighbours and anyone who needs a rest. Transport improvements should make ordinary journeys easier for a wider range of people.

questions.prompt: Who changed their opinion after seeing the results of a trial?
Who values a predictable journey time most?
Who wants a ticket suitable for infrequent journeys?
Who became a regular bus user after a timetable change?
Who supports a restriction only if exceptions are made?
Who says the same travel choice will not suit everyone?
Who would accept a higher fare for a dependable service?

items.title: The library of useful things
items.prompt: Read the article and choose the best heading for each paragraph. Use each heading once. One heading is not needed.

passages.heading: A
passages.text: When a small town library announced that it would lend household tools as well as books, the first reaction was amusement. Why would anyone borrow a drill from a librarian? Yet the idea came from a familiar problem: residents often bought equipment for a single job and then left it unused for years. The library already had a trusted system for lending things, and its staff wondered whether that system could serve a different kind of need. The proposal was not to turn the building into a shop. It was to make occasional use of useful objects possible without requiring everyone to own them.

passages.heading: B
passages.text: The team began by asking residents which objects they actually needed. Staff expected gardening equipment to dominate, but the replies were much more varied. People requested sewing machines, basic repair tools and equipment for small community events. Several popular suggestions were rejected because the objects would be too dangerous or difficult to maintain. Instead of ordering a large collection immediately, the library borrowed a few items from local organisations and ran a short trial. This gave staff a chance to observe demand rather than relying entirely on what people said they might use. The final starting collection was smaller and more practical than the original wish list.

passages.heading: C
passages.text: Owning the objects turned out to be the easy part. Each returned item had to be checked, cleaned and, occasionally, repaired before it could be lent again. A damaged cable could make an otherwise ordinary tool unsafe. At first, the librarians tried to fit these checks around their existing duties, but queues quickly formed at the desk. A local technician later agreed to inspect the equipment on fixed afternoons. The schedule meant that some items could not be borrowed immediately after being returned, but it made the service more dependable. Behind the simple act of borrowing lay a new routine that visitors rarely noticed.

passages.heading: D
passages.text: Staff also discovered that access did not always lead to use. Some visitors wanted to borrow a sewing machine but were unsure how to start. Others worried that they would damage an unfamiliar tool. In response, the library introduced short introductory sessions led by experienced volunteers. These were not intended to make anyone an expert; they covered basic operation and explained when professional help was more appropriate. Attendance at the sessions increased borrowing, but it also changed the atmosphere. People began asking one another for advice, and a service originally designed around objects started creating connections between residents who had never previously spoken.

passages.heading: E
passages.text: The project was often described as an environmental success because fewer people needed to buy new equipment. The organisers were pleased by the interest but cautious about the claim. Borrowing only reduces new purchases if people would otherwise have bought something. It may also involve extra journeys, and heavily used items need replacement. To understand the actual effect, the library began asking borrowers what they would have done without the service and how they travelled to collect equipment. The answers did not produce a simple slogan. They did, however, provide a more useful basis for deciding which objects to offer and how to organise collection.

passages.heading: F
passages.text: Funding created another difficult choice. A small charge for every loan would help cover repairs, yet it might discourage residents with the least money. Making everything free would keep access simple but leave the service dependent on donations. After consulting users, the library chose a mixed approach: basic items remained free, while optional training workshops carried a modest fee. A local business contributed to maintenance costs without choosing which products the library purchased. The arrangement was not a permanent solution, and staff planned to review it each year. Its purpose was to share costs without allowing the need for income to replace the service’s original aim.

passages.heading: G
passages.text: Other towns soon asked for instructions so that they could copy the project. The organisers shared their records but warned against copying the collection exactly. A neighbourhood with many small flats would have different needs from one with large gardens. Staff time, transport and access to repair skills would differ too. The most useful lesson was therefore a process rather than a shopping list: start with a limited trial, listen to users, record problems and adjust. Expansion should follow evidence that the service is useful and manageable. A larger collection might look impressive in a photograph, but it would mean little if the objects were rarely borrowed or safely maintained.
